claims.text: Electroless deposition can produce a continuous nanoscale Cu shell on W powders.
Cu-coated W powders followed by SPS will form a continuous Cu network.
Cu-coated W powders followed by SPS will produce fully wetted W/Cu interfaces and eliminate interfacial voids.
The Cu-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an identically processed SPS composite made from uncoated powders.
A Cu-shell thickness of approximately 100–200 nm is suitable for the proposed W and Cu powder sizes.
SPS at 1000–1100 °C, 50 MPa, for 10 minutes in vacuum is an effective processing schedule for the coated W–Cu powders.
The nanoscale Cu shell melts during SPS.
Molten Cu from the shell flows between and wets neighboring W particles.
Flow and wetting by the Cu shell eliminate voids and promote densification.
The proposed liquid-Cu-assisted densification occurs without W grain growth.
The resulting microstructure has minimal porosity and maximized Cu conduction pathways.
Relative to uncoated-powder SPS, Cu-shell plating will increase composite thermal conductivity by at least 30%.
Relative to uncoated-powder SPS, Cu-shell plating will reduce open porosity to below 2 vol%.
The proposed mechanism and benefits remain valid over SPS temperatures of 950–1150 °C and pressures of 30–70 MPa.
The resulting composite is suitable for service in vacuum or inert environments at 500–900 °C under irradiation up to 10 dpa.
The resulting composite can tolerate thermal fluxes up to 10 MW/m².
The degree of improvement depends on Cu-shell uniformity and continuity and on Cu evaporation or oxidation during SPS.

contradictions.description: The primary prediction requires at least a 30% conductivity increase and porosity below 2 vol%, whereas the falsification rule accepts the weaker thresholds of at least a 20% increase and porosity at or below 4 vol%. Results between these thresholds would fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.

The mechanism requires the Cu shell to liquefy, but the proposed processing range extends down to 950 °C and the controlled experiment uses 1050 °C; these temperatures are below the approximately 1085 °C melting point of Cu. Thus, liquefaction cannot operate across the full stated range or in the specified experiment absent an unmentioned melting-point-depression mechanism.
